title: HPV Vaccine Cuts Risk of Head, Neck, and Other Cancers, Studies Show
excerpt: New research finds the vaccine protects against cancers well beyond the cervix, with vaccinated men and boys nearly 50% less likely to develop several HPV-related malignancies.
body:
• Men and boys vaccinated between ages 9 and 26 were nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head, neck, esophagus, anus, or penis, according to a JAMA Oncology study of more than 1 million participants.
  • A separate study of 1.4 million US medical records found HPV vaccination reduced head and neck cancer risk by 68% and oropharyngeal cancer risk by 91%.
  • A 274-study evidence review confirms the vaccine cuts cervical cancer risk by 80% in women vaccinated by age 16, with protection lasting at least 16 years.
  • Experts say the vaccine may matter even more for oral and throat cancers, which have no screening tests and are often caught late.

The HPV vaccine, developed two decades ago to fight cervical cancer, is proving to be a far broader weapon against cancer than its creators anticipated.

A series of studies published in 2025 and 2026 show the vaccine sharply reduces the risk of cancers of the head, neck, throat, esophagus, penis, vagina, vulva, and anus — leading researchers to call it potentially more transformative for cancers that lack early detection tools.

Nearly 50% Risk Reduction in Men and Boys

Men and boys who received the HPV vaccine between ages 9 and 26 were nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, anus, or penis, according to a study published in JAMA Oncology in April 2026. The research, led by Taito Kitano, DrPH, of Nara Prefecture General Medical Center in Japan, analyzed data from more than 510,000 vaccinated males and an equal number of unvaccinated males, covering vaccinations administered from January 2016 through December 2024.

"Children, adolescents, parents and health care workers should be more informed about the expected benefits of HPV vaccine, not just cervical cancer," Kitano said.

"This is a vaccine that is preventing cancer in a major way."

— Oliver Brooks, MD, National Foundation for Infectious Diseases

A separate study published in August 2026 in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases reinforced those findings. Researchers led by Ching-Nung Wu, MD, PhD, of Kaohsiung Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taiwan analyzed 1.4 million medical records from 66 US healthcare organizations. People vaccinated between ages 9 and 26 were 68% less likely to be diagnosed with head or neck cancer — and 91% less likely to develop oropharyngeal cancers, which affect the tonsils, base of the tongue, and back of the throat.

Why Oral and Throat Cancers May Be the Bigger Breakthrough

Unlike cervical cancer, which can be caught through routine screening, head and neck cancers have no early detection tests and are typically diagnosed only after patients develop pain or swelling — often at advanced stages when treatment is more difficult.

"HPV vaccines could be even more of a game-changer for these other cancers than for cervical cancer," said Otis Brawley, MD, a professor of oncology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.

In 2018, the CDC reported that oral and throat cancer had become the most common HPV-related malignancy in the United States. HPV now causes roughly 70% of head and neck cancers, most of which develop in the oropharynx.

80% Cervical Cancer Reduction, 16+ Years of Protection

A comprehensive evidence review published by the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project in 2026 evaluated 274 studies and confirmed the vaccine reduces cervical cancer risk by 80% in women vaccinated by age 16 and 66% in those vaccinated later. Protection has been documented for up to 16 years after vaccination.

The review also found no evidence of serious side effects, based on more than 300 million doses administered worldwide.

"The data show how important HPV vaccination is to prevent persistent HPV infections that lead to cancer."

— Angela Ulrich, PhD, CIDRAP Director of Research

A December 2025 study separately found that women who received at least one dose were 37% less likely to develop precancerous lesions of the vagina or vulva.

Herd Immunity and Stalled Coverage

Emerging research suggests HPV vaccines have created herd immunity, reducing viral circulation enough to protect even unvaccinated individuals. Declining rates of HPV infection, cervical precancers, and genital warts among unvaccinated populations support this conclusion.

But vaccination rates in the United States have plateaued. CDC data show 78.2% of 13-to-17-year-olds have received at least one dose, while only 62.9% have completed the full recommended series — figures unchanged from 2022 to 2024. Nearly 40,000 Americans are diagnosed with an HPV-related cancer each year.

Cervical cancer incidence fell 65% from 2012 to 2019 among US women under 25. In the same age group, cervical cancer deaths declined 62% from 2013–2015 to 2019–2021. Current vaccines protect against nine viral strains that together cause 90% of cervical cancers.
